title: Seneca gets seasick
hook: Seneca gets so seasick he jumps overboard; our faults are hidden until we recover (Letters 53)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the dark house, Harpaste's story. Your line was the dark is in me. Did you catch an it's-not-my-fault sentence before it finished? Day four hundred sixty-five.
screen: `THE DARK HOUSE — THE DARK IS IN ME.`

segments.voice: The sea looks calm. Seneca, who should know better, lets himself be talked into a short boat trip along the coast near Naples, from one town to the next. Halfway across, the sky turns, the swell builds, and the great philosopher of calm becomes very, very sick. He begs the pilot to put him ashore. The pilot says there's nowhere to land. What happens next is the most undignified scene in the letters, told by the man himself, and he tells it on purpose. Today: Seneca gets seasick.
screen: `A CALM SEA, A SHORT TRIP.` → `THE SWELL BUILDS.` → `THE PHILOSOPHER OF CALM, VERY SICK.`

segments.voice: First, the jump. The pilot won't steer for the rocky shore, so Seneca, an old lover of cold water since his youth, throws himself into the sea and swims for land, crawling up the rocks. Only then, he says, did he understand that seasickness doesn't leave you just because you've reached dry ground. Second, the body tells you. A sick body sends signals, he notes: a heavy ache, a fever creeping in. You can't miss them for long. Third, the soul hides it. Faults of the mind are the opposite. The worse they are, the less we feel them. Someone lightly asleep notices their dreams, and sometimes knows they're dreaming. Someone in a deep sleep doesn't even know they're asleep. Why does nobody confess their faults? Because they're still in them. Telling your dream is for someone who's awake. Fourth, the sign of health. So Seneca says: admitting your faults is a sign of returning health. In Latin, vitia sua confiteri sanitatis indicium est. The moment you can say, oh, that's what I do when I'm afraid, you're already climbing up the rocks. It's not a failure to notice a fault. It's a sign that the fever is breaking.
screen: `SENECA JUMPS OVERBOARD.` · `THE BODY SENDS SIGNALS.` · `THE SOUL'S FAULTS HIDE.` · `ADMITTING IT IS HEALTH.` · then, large: `AWAKE TO IT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Let the last few days pass in front of you like the coast from a boat. Look for one fault you've only just noticed, something you didn't see a week ago: maybe a way you interrupt, or a way you go quiet, or a small habit of exaggerating. Name it plainly, once, inside. Then notice the strange relief that comes with naming. That's what being awake feels like. The bell holds the time.
Seneca gets seasick. In the fifty-third letter, he jumps overboard, and learns that the soul's faults hide like deep sleep; confessing them is a sign of health. Today's word.
Your line: awake to it. Today, if someone points out a fault of yours, try one honest sentence back: you might be right. Day four hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Readers of Seneca often treat noticing a new fault as progress rather than failure, and some keep a brief note of faults they have recently become aware of.

trapdoor: what you thought: a funny travel story.
what it means: soul faults hide like deep sleep, and seeing them is the first sign of waking.
what a scholar hears: Letters 53.1–8; the trip is from Parthenope (Naples) toward Puteoli; 'vetus frigidae cultor' is Seneca's self-description as a lover of cold water.

sources.quoted: vitia sua confiteri sanitatis indicium est

notes: Letters 53.1–4: the voyage from Parthenope to Puteoli, the pilot's refusal, Seneca's leap ('vetus frigidae cultor'), climbing the rocks, and that nausea persisted on land. Confirm.

53.5–8: bodily illness signals vs hidden diseases of the soul, the light and deep sleep image, 'somnium narrare vigilantis est', 'vitia sua confiteri sanitatis indicium est'. Confirm wording and numbering.
Note: Seneca was in fact aged (he was in his sixties) when this happened; the script doesn't give his age.
